title: SYSK Selects: How Electroconvulsive Therapy Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2013 episode on electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Josh introduces it as an eye-opening episode originally released May 2013. The hosts discuss Ken Kesey's One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest and how ECT was misused in asylums as a means of control, then cover the history of shock therapies: Ladislaus von Meduna's insulin coma, Manfred Sakel's Metrazol shock, and the Italian scientists who introduced electricity in the 1930s. They describe modern ECT practice (anesthesia, muscle relaxants, pulse settings, pre-treatment screening, treatment schedule), FDA device classification, its use for severe depression, the decline in England with the rise of antidepressants, theories of how it works, a Scottish brain-scan study, memory loss and mortality risks. The episode closes with listener mail about misheard song lyrics.

entities.name: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
Shock: The Healing Powers of Electro Convulsive Therapy

segments.title: Selects intro and show opening
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick, saying the episode first aired in May 2013 and changed his view of ECT as merely a barbaric control tool. The hosts open the show with banter about One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.
topics: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest

segments.title: ECT misuse in asylums and modern acceptance
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how asylums in the mid-20th century used electroconvulsive therapy to control patients, as depicted in Kesey's novel, and how that misuse gave ECT a bad reputation. They note that ECT is now endorsed by the NIMH, APA, AMA and Surgeon General for severe depression, and mention Kitty Dukakis's book Shock and about 100,000 Americans treated per year.

segments.title: What shock therapy aims to do
segments.summary: Josh explains that the term electroshock is loosely accurate, and that shock therapies aim to induce a seizure or convulsion. Hippocrates reportedly noticed patients improved after convulsions. The hosts note no one knows exactly why it works and compare it to catharsis.

segments.title: History: insulin and Metrazol shock
segments.summary: The hosts describe early experiments with insulin shock by Hungarian physician Ladislaus von Meduna, who believed seizures had a curative effect and wrongly claimed schizophrenia and epilepsy could not coexist. They then cover Manfred Sakel's Metrazol-induced seizures, which were powerful but caused spinal fractures.

segments.title: Introduction of electricity and early use
segments.summary: Italian scientists in the 1930s used electricity to induce seizures, reporting that delusions receded after several treatments. Within a few years it was used regularly in the US for schizophrenia, depression and bipolar disorder. Early treatments were given without anesthesia.

segments.title: Modern ECT procedure and safety
segments.summary: The hosts describe modern practice: anesthesia, muscle relaxants, a blood pressure cuff on the ankle to keep one foot from convulsing, pre-treatment screening, brief pulses (shorter pulse widths now used), and a typical schedule of two to three sessions weekly for three to four weeks. They discuss the FDA Class III classification and the memory loss that is still associated with treatment, contrasted with the zombie-like portrayals in popular culture.

segments.title: Use for depression, antidepressants and how it works
segments.summary: The hosts say ECT is effective for about 80 percent of people with severe depression who have not responded to drugs. They note UK use fell by half from 1985 to 2002 as antidepressants rose, and that ECT may extend antidepressant effects. Theories of how it works include changes to blood flow, metabolism and chemical release, described as a brain reset. A 2012 Scottish brain-scan study and a placebo-controlled finding are discussed.

segments.title: Risks, mortality and closing thoughts
segments.summary: The hosts review risks: two types of memory loss (around the appointment, usually fading, and longer-term loss of past events), a mortality rate of about one in ten thousand patients usually tied to anesthesia, headaches and muscle pain. They note critics who are anti-psychiatry, and close with thoughts on electricity versus drugs.

segments.title: Listener mail: misheard song lyrics
segments.summary: The hosts read listener mail about misheard song lyrics, including Cheryl's 'Papa Don't Preach' as 'Papa Dom bridge' and a note about Until Tuesday opening a concert. The episode ends with a call for marriage stories.
